heading: PROPHET YŪSUF (AS)
title: THE BEAUTY OF PATIENCE AND FORGIVENESS
themes: Truth • Self-Restraint • Tawḥīd • Foresight • Responsibility • Mercy
scope: 10 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 10 SELECTED ĀYĀT
introduction: This tenth world continues directly from Volume Nine, in which Imaan and Akhlaq studied Prophet Isḥāq and Prophet Yaʿqūb (peace be upon them). Dadi Jaan’s final card said that the next story begins with a dream. The new world follows Prophet Yūsuf (AS), son of Yaʿqūb (AS), as recounted in Sūrah Yūsuf. It traces the dream, the brothers’ jealousy, separation, steadfastness in Egypt, imprisonment, interpretation of dreams, stewardship, family reunion, forgiveness and Yūsuf’s prayer.

The children’s modern adventures are original fiction. Imaan, Akhlaq, Salaam, Salamah, Dadi Jaan, Sheikh Uncle, Sir Zameer, Mohsin and Mohsina never witness, join, impersonate or alter Prophetic events. The sacred account is taught from Qur’anic passages and reviewed classical explanation; the academy and family stories show separate, limited applications.

blocks.text: The family tree had hardly been rolled away when Akhlaq found a golden card beneath it. Eleven tiny stars circled a sun and moon. On the back Dadi Jaan had written: THE NEXT STORY BEGINS WITH A DREAM. He rushed to the breakfast table before anybody had finished eating. “Is it a puzzle?” he asked. “It is a passage of the Qur’an,” Dadi replied, opening Sūrah Yūsuf.

She told the children only what the verses established: Yūsuf had told his father Yaʿqūb of his remarkable dream, and his father advised him not to share it with his brothers because of the danger of plotting. “Was his father teaching him to lie?” Imaan asked. “No,” Dadi said. “Wise privacy is not falsehood. Nor does it mean you should keep danger secret.”

At school, Mohsina quietly told Imaan she was worried about a presentation. At lunch another child asked what Mohsina had said. Imaan was tempted to share the detail so everyone would know she was a close friend. Instead she replied that Mohsina was preparing and might appreciate encouragement. Later, when a younger pupil described a frightening threat, Imaan immediately approached Sir Zameer for help.

Akhlaq watched the difference. One conversation deserved discretion. The other required protection. At home he drew a small door on his notebook. Above it he wrote: ASK BEFORE SHARING. Beneath it: ASK FOR HELP WHEN SOMEONE IS UNSAFE. Dadi Jaan approved. “Now we may study what happens when jealousy overcomes good judgment.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Privacy needs wisdom, and danger must always be reported to a trustworthy adult.

stories.title: The Bitter Seed
stories.subtitle: Jealousy is a feeling to manage, not a command to obey

blocks.text: An announcement appeared at Sheikh Uncle’s Academy: two teams would represent the school at the reading exhibition. Mohsin’s group was selected. Akhlaq congratulated him, but the words felt heavy. He had worked hard, too. That afternoon he could not stop staring at the noticeboard.

Sheikh Uncle found him beside the display. “It can hurt when you hoped for something and someone else receives it,” he said. “The test is what you choose next.” Then he explained that Sūrah Yūsuf describes the brothers’ jealousy and their terrible plan. Their conduct was wrongdoing; the Qur’an does not ask readers to admire or imitate it.

Back in class, Akhlaq nearly suggested that Mohsin had won only because a teacher liked him. Imaan asked whether he had any evidence. He had none. She reminded him that an untrue rumour could damage a friendship. Mohsin arrived carrying a box of books, unaware of the conversation. Akhlaq offered to help him sort them. The jealousy did not vanish at once, but the dishonest sentence remained unsaid.

After the exhibition, Akhlaq wrote two columns in his notebook: WHAT I FEEL and WHAT I CHOOSE. Under the first he wrote “disappointed.” Under the second: “tell the truth, practise, congratulate, and ask what I can improve.” Dadi said that naming a feeling honestly was useful; making another person suffer because of it was not.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Jealousy must not become injustice; choose truthful, generous conduct.

stories.title: The Story That Did Not Fit
stories.subtitle: An accusation is not evidence

blocks.text: On Monday a parcel of drawing cards disappeared from the academy cupboard. Someone whispered that a younger pupil must have taken it. Within minutes the whisper had travelled across three classrooms. Akhlaq wanted to confront the child. “Everybody knows,” he said. Sir Zameer answered, “Everybody repeating something does not make it true.”

The teacher first made sure the class was calm and nobody was threatened. Then he checked the delivery record and discovered that the parcel had been moved to another room for safekeeping. The younger pupil had done nothing wrong. Akhlaq felt deeply ashamed. Mohsina asked him to help correct the rumour with the same energy he had given to repeating it.

In their Qur’an lesson, Dadi explained the false account brought to Yaʿqūb concerning Yūsuf. She read Sūrah Yūsuf 12:18, emphasizing that the brothers’ false report formed part of a grave family trial and was not equivalent to a misplaced school parcel. The smaller lesson for the children was evidence, honesty and restraint: do not invent certainty when you do not know.

Akhlaq found the younger pupil and apologised without asking for instant forgiveness. He told his classmates that the rumour had been incorrect and that he should never have repeated it. That night the compass lay beside his notebook, pointing nowhere remarkable. The useful direction was his new sentence: WHEN THE FACTS ARE MISSING, STOP THE RUMOUR.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: An accusation needs evidence; correct harmful rumours promptly.

stories.title: The Door That Must Stay Closed
stories.subtitle: Integrity needs both courage and help

blocks.text: Rain cancelled the outdoor games. At the academy, a few older pupils suggested changing the scores in a practice competition so their group would receive a certificate. “Nobody checks these,” one said. Akhlaq was uncomfortable. He wanted to be included, but he knew the proposal was dishonest.

He stepped away and spoke to Sir Zameer. The teacher thanked him, kept the report confidential as appropriate, and made sure he would not face retaliation. Later the class studied Yūsuf’s steadfastness when he faced coercion and wrongdoing in Egypt. Sheikh Uncle explained the relevant passage gently: Yūsuf sought Allah’s protection and chose righteousness even when he faced severe pressure. The sacred episode was far more serious than a school rule being broken.

“What if somebody powerful makes a child feel unsafe?” Mohsina asked. Salamah, visiting for a family-learning day, answered carefully. “The child is not to blame. They should get away if they can, tell a trustworthy adult, and keep seeking help until someone protects them.” No child was asked to discuss a private experience in front of the class.

At home, Imaan drew a strong line across a page: SAY NO TO WRONG, SEEK HELP, STAY SAFE. Akhlaq realised that courage was not a demand to face danger alone. Sometimes courage meant asking the right person to intervene.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Refuse wrongdoing, protect boundaries and seek trustworthy help.

stories.title: Hope Inside Difficult Days
stories.subtitle: Useful service can continue during hardship

blocks.text: The school library renovation lasted longer than expected. Books were stacked in boxes, the reading corner closed, and the younger pupils complained that nothing interesting was available. Mohsin proposed that the student volunteers stop coming until everything was ready. “We cannot fix the building,” he said.

Imaan suggested a travelling book basket instead. With the teacher’s approval, the group sorted books into safe small sets and delivered them to classrooms. Akhlaq made labels; Mohsina prepared a simple borrowing register. Their work did not make the renovation disappear, but it made the difficult days more bearable for other people.

Dadi Jaan later described Yūsuf’s years of difficulty and imprisonment. The Qur’an records that, while imprisoned, he spoke to fellow prisoners and called them to the worship of Allah alone. She did not invent an exact count of years, dialogue or prison scenes. “His trust in Allah did not depend on comfortable circumstances,” she said.

At the end of the week a younger child returned a book with a thank-you note. Akhlaq looked at the tired volunteers and smiled. They had not won a competition or solved every problem. They had found one useful thing they could responsibly do. He wrote: HARD DAYS DO NOT CANCEL GOOD DEEDS.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Difficulty does not prevent safe, sincere, useful service.

A small school garden produced more vegetables than the kitchen could use that morning. Akhlaq suggested distributing everything at once. Mohsina noticed that several baskets would spoil before anyone could collect them. Sir Zameer invited the children to make a sensible plan with the gardeners: give suitable portions now, preserve what could safely be stored, and check what would be needed next week.

In their next lesson, Sheikh Uncle related the king’s dream and the knowledge Allah granted Yūsuf to interpret it. Sūrah Yūsuf describes years of plentiful crops followed by difficult years. Yūsuf’s advice included storing much of the harvest in its ears. It was a specific historical example of foresight and provision; the children were not pretending to be Yūsuf or to predict the future.

Their garden team created three labels: USE NOW, STORE SAFELY and SHARE RESPONSIBLY. Mohsin wanted to call the activity “The Seven-Year Challenge,” but Imaan said they should simply learn the principle without playing at a Prophet’s task. Everyone agreed.

When the school later held a community meal, enough produce remained to help. Akhlaq understood that generosity and planning did not compete. Good intentions become more helpful when paired with accurate information and wise preparation.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Careful planning is part of responsible action.

Sheikh Uncle’s Academy needed a volunteer to oversee the exhibition materials. Some children nominated the loudest speaker. Others chose the person who had won the most certificates. Imaan asked a different question: “Who can keep careful records and make sure everyone receives what they need?”

Sir Zameer used the moment to explain Yūsuf’s appointment over the storehouses in Egypt. Sūrah Yūsuf records that he described himself as reliable and knowledgeable for that responsibility. Prophetic authority is not an app prize, and public service is not a popularity contest. The limited lesson was the importance of honest competence.

The class selected a small team instead of awarding a title to one child. Akhlaq counted the materials. Mohsina checked access for younger pupils. Mohsin managed the carrying plan, and Imaan wrote the record. On the first afternoon Akhlaq counted the same box twice; he corrected the record rather than hiding it.

By the exhibition day nobody had a crown, a grand chair or a special badge. Everything was in the right place, and the youngest children were able to participate. Dadi Jaan asked Akhlaq what the team had achieved. “We kept the trust,” he answered, “even when there was no applause.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Trust is fulfilled through honesty, competence and service.

stories.title: The Visit and the Unanswered Questions
stories.subtitle: Fairness includes caution and kindness

blocks.text: Two groups wanted the same academy room for their presentations. One had booked it early; the other needed extra space because one pupil used mobility equipment. The children quickly divided into competing sides. “Our group is right,” Akhlaq said, although he had not read either booking request.

Sir Zameer invited both groups to explain their needs. The schedule was adjusted without mocking anyone, and an accessible room was secured. “Fairness needs information,” he said. “It also needs care for those affected.”

During their reading, the children followed the later part of Sūrah Yūsuf, when the brothers came to Egypt and did not recognise Yūsuf. Dadi carefully followed the Qur’anic sequence of visits and questions, without turning the brothers’ distress into a pursuit game or claiming knowledge of motives not established by the text.

Mohsina asked whether every difficult family relationship could be repaired immediately. Salamah replied that trust can require time, truthful behaviour and wise boundaries. The children wrote on their poster: DO NOT RUSH TO JUDGE; DO NOT IGNORE PEOPLE’S SAFETY. Akhlaq realised that a wise decision is sometimes more patient than a quick victory.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Good judgment joins fairness with caution and care.

When the academy’s final exhibition poster was printed, Akhlaq noticed that Mohsin’s contribution had been left out of the credits. He had been responsible for checking the names. He thought of blaming the printer, but he remembered how rumours had once harmed a younger pupil.

He found Mohsin before the exhibition opened. “I did not check carefully,” he said. “I am sorry. I will ask Sir Zameer to correct the display.” Mohsin was upset and needed some time. Akhlaq accepted that an apology could not command immediate comfort.

In the Qur’anic account, Yūsuf’s brothers eventually acknowledged wrongdoing. Yūsuf’s response, preserved in Sūrah Yūsuf, included mercy and forgiveness. Dadi said this was not permission to conceal harm or to pressure a child to reconcile with someone unsafe. Repentance includes turning away from wrongdoing; repairing harm may require adults and practical safeguards.

After the corrected credits were posted, Mohsin thanked Akhlaq for speaking honestly. Their friendship felt less brittle because the mistake had been faced rather than concealed. That night Akhlaq wrote: AN APOLOGY HAS WORDS, AND IT ALSO HAS WORK.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Admit wrongdoing, repair harm and respect others’ boundaries.

stories.title: The Last Leaf on the Family Tree
stories.subtitle: A legacy of faith becomes a living choice

blocks.text: The final gathering at Sheikh Uncle’s Academy was quiet rather than grand. Imaan and Akhlaq brought the family-tree poster from Volume Nine, now extended to include Yūsuf beneath Yaʿqūb. Around it were leaves bearing words gathered during the world: TRUST, TRUTH, COURAGE, TAWḤĪD, PREPARATION, RESPONSIBILITY, PATIENCE, MERCY.

Sheikh Uncle reminded the families that Sūrah Yūsuf leads to reunion and the explanation of the original dream. The Qur’an records Yūsuf’s gratitude to Allah and his prayer concerning faith and the Hereafter. The reunion was Allah’s blessing within that specific history, not a promise that every painful family situation will end in the same worldly way.

Each visitor chose one small practice to continue. A child chose to stop repeating rumours. A mother chose to give a worried child more time to speak. A father promised to apologise when he made a mistake. Mohsina chose to check whether her group’s activities included everyone. Nobody was asked to reveal private family troubles or prove their goodness for a score.

When Akhlaq looked at the golden card with eleven stars, it no longer seemed a puzzle about secret knowledge. “The dream began a story,” he said, “but the lessons can continue in our choices.” Imaan added one last leaf: REMEMBER ALLAH IN EVERY SEASON. Dadi Jaan left a fresh blank space for the next world.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Gratitude to Allah should shape the choices we continue making.

review.arabic: إِذْ قَالَ يُوسُفُ لِأَبِيهِ يَا أَبَتِ إِنِّي رَأَيْتُ أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا وَالشَّمْسَ وَالْقَمَرَ رَأَيْتُهُمْ لِي سَاجِدِينَ
review.meaning: Yūsuf told his father that he had seen eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to him.

review.arabic: قَالَ يَا بُنَيَّ لَا تَقْصُصْ رُؤْيَاكَ عَلَىٰ إِخْوَتِكَ فَيَكِيدُوا لَكَ كَيْدًا ۖ إِنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ لِلْإِنْسَانِ عَدُوٌّ مُبِينٌ
review.meaning: Yaʿqūb advised his son not to relate this particular dream to his brothers, warning of possible plotting.

review.arabic: وَجَاءُوا عَلَىٰ قَمِيصِهِ بِدَمٍ كَذِبٍ ۚ قَالَ بَلْ سَوَّلَتْ لَكُمْ أَنْفُسُكُمْ أَمْرًا ۖ فَصَبْرٌ جَمِيلٌ ۖ وَاللَّهُ الْمُسْتَعَانُ عَلَىٰ مَا تَصِفُونَ
review.meaning: The brothers brought a shirt with false blood; Yaʿqūb sought beautiful patience and Allah’s help.

review.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ السِّجْنُ أَحَبُّ إِلَيَّ مِمَّا يَدْعُونَنِي إِلَيْهِ ۖ وَإِلَّا تَصْرِفْ عَنِّي كَيْدَهُنَّ أَصْبُ إِلَيْهِنَّ وَأَكُنْ مِنَ الْجَاهِلِينَ
review.meaning: Yūsuf prayed to Allah for protection from wrongdoing, even in the face of serious consequences.

review.arabic: قَالَ تَزْرَعُونَ سَبْعَ سِنِينَ دَأَبًا فَمَا حَصَدْتُمْ فَذَرُوهُ فِي سُنْبُلِهِ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِمَّا تَأْكُلُونَ
review.meaning: Yūsuf explained a plan for years of planting and conserving the harvest.

review.arabic: قَالَ اجْعَلْنِي عَلَىٰ خَزَائِنِ الْأَرْضِ ۖ إِنِّي حَفِيظٌ عَلِيمٌ
review.meaning: Yūsuf offered himself for responsibility over the storehouses, describing his trustworthiness and knowledge.

review.arabic: قَالَ إِنَّمَا أَشْكُو بَثِّي وَحُزْنِي إِلَى اللَّهِ وَأَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ
review.meaning: Yaʿqūb expressed his deep sorrow to Allah.

review.arabic: يَا بَنِيَّ اذْهَبُوا فَتَحَسَّسُوا مِنْ يُوسُفَ وَأَخِيهِ وَلَا تَيْأَسُوا مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّهُ لَا يَيْأَسُ مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ إِلَّا الْقَوْمُ الْكَافِرُونَ
review.meaning: Yaʿqūb told his sons to seek Yūsuf and his brother and not despair of Allah’s relief.

review.arabic: قَالُوا أَإِنَّكَ لَأَنْتَ يُوسُفُ ۖ قَالَ أَنَا يُوسُفُ وَهَٰذَا أَخِي ۖ قَدْ مَنَّ اللَّهُ عَلَيْنَا ۖ إِنَّهُ مَنْ يَتَّقِ وَيَصْبِرْ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُضِيعُ أَجْرَ الْمُحْسِنِينَ
review.meaning: Yūsuf identified himself and connected patience and mindfulness of Allah with doing good.

review.arabic: قَالَ لَا تَثْرِيبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْيَوْمَ ۖ يَغْفِرُ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ ۖ وَهُوَ أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ
review.meaning: Yūsuf spoke words of forgiveness toward his brothers and invoked Allah’s mercy.

synthesis.text: The dream was not the end of the story

Sūrah Yūsuf opens with a remarkable dream but does not present a simple tale of instant success. It describes envy, wrongdoing, separation and profound difficulty, while Allah’s knowledge and wisdom remain beyond what the characters initially understand. The full story must be read as revelation, not reduced to a self-improvement formula that guarantees a child the same outward outcome.
Steadfastness in places of pressure

Yūsuf’s response to coercion and injustice is a central lesson in faith and moral courage. His prayer and reliance upon Allah must be taught without suggesting that vulnerable children are responsible for what others do to them. The ethical application for children is to respect boundaries, reject wrongdoing when safe, and seek protective adult help.
Knowledge, preparation and service

The interpretation of the king’s dream and the stewardship of Egypt’s resources show that the knowledge Allah bestowed on Yūsuf was connected with careful provision. In our school-life applications, children may practise planning, honest recordkeeping and fair distribution without playing at the Prophet’s authority or claiming prophetic insight.
Patience, sorrow and hope

Yaʿqūb’s sadness and continued hope demonstrate that grief is not proof of weak faith. Seeking Allah’s help and taking practical steps are compatible. The app must never punish sad feelings or assume that all loss is soon repaired. A child facing harm or overwhelming distress should receive adult support rather than a private score.
Forgiveness is beautiful, and safety still matters

The reunion and Yūsuf’s generous words to his brothers show remarkable mercy. Children can learn to admit wrong, restore what they have harmed and forgive when appropriate. Forgiveness should not be used to force unsafe contact, to excuse repeated harm or to silence someone seeking help. The final lasting lesson is sincere gratitude to Allah and responsibility in everyday conduct.

CARRY FORWARD • Be truthful. Guard trust. Resist envy. Seek Allah’s help. Protect boundaries. Plan wisely. Repair harm. Practise mercy without compromising safety. Remember Allah in success and difficulty.
